title: Landmark reports that changed practice
blurb: Trace the reports and scandals that exposed unequal care for people with a learning disability, and the lessons every nurse should carry.
question: A ward sister asks her learning disability liaison nurse which theme runs through Death by Indifference, CIPOLD and LeDeR, so she can use it in staff training. What is the best answer?

teach.body: Over two decades, a series of reports showed that people with a learning disability were dying younger, often from causes that good health care could have prevented, and that some were abused in closed services. Each report led to new policy. In plain English: today's reasonable adjustments, mortality reviews and training exist because these people's stories were told, and nurses carry the lessons into every shift.

teach.caption: CIPOLD recommended a national mortality review body; this became LeDeR.

teach.h: Death by Indifference and Healthcare for All
teach.body: In 2007 Mencap's Death by Indifference told the stories of six people with a learning disability who died in NHS care. It led to an independent inquiry chaired by Sir Jonathan Michael, Healthcare for All (2008), which examined why people with a learning disability received worse health care. The lesson: indifference, poor communication and failure to listen to families can be fatal.

teach.h: Winterbourne View to Building the Right Support

teach.body: Bethan, a ward manager, asks the liaison nurse for one message from the reports. The nurse explains that Death by Indifference, CIPOLD and LeDeR all describe delays in diagnosis and treatment, and families' concerns being ignored. She builds training around three actions: treat a change from the person's baseline as possible illness, listen to and act on what carers say, and plan reasonable adjustments before tests and treatment.

teach.h: Recurring themes and the nursing response
head: Theme in the reports
Your response
rows: Ask, record and act on carer concern
Symptoms put down to the disability

teach.text: Do not mix up the reports. Death by Indifference (Mencap, 2007) told six stories; Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry that followed; CIPOLD (2013) measured premature deaths (13 years men, 20 years women) and led to LeDeR. Winterbourne View (2011) led to Transforming Care, not to LeDeR.

items: Death by Indifference (Mencap 2007): six deaths in NHS care; led to Healthcare for All (2008).
CIPOLD (2013): men 13 and women 20 years earlier; 37% vs 13% deaths amenable to good care; led to LeDeR.
Winterbourne View (2011) led to Transforming Care (2012) and Building the Right Support (2015).
BRS action plan target to halve inpatients by March 2024 was missed (2,055 in Feb 2025, down 29%).
Common theme: delays and families not listened to.

summary: You can now place the major learning disability reports in order, quote CIPOLD's key figures, and link Winterbourne View to Transforming Care and Building the Right Support. You can also turn their recurring themes into everyday nursing actions.

A.q: Tunde, a student learning disability nurse, is writing about the 2007 Mencap report that described the deaths of six people with a learning disability in NHS care. Which report is this?
options: Healthcare for All
Death by Indifference
Valuing People
Transforming Care
A.why: Death by Indifference (Mencap, 2007) told the stories of six people with a learning disability who died in NHS care.

whyNot.0: Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry that followed it.
whyNot.2: Valuing People (2001) was a government white paper setting policy principles.
whyNot.3: Transforming Care followed Winterbourne View in 2012.

A.q: Which independent inquiry, chaired by Sir Jonathan Michael, followed Death by Indifference?
options: CIPOLD
Building the Right Support
Healthcare for All
The LeDeR programme
A.why: Healthcare for All (2008) was the independent inquiry into access to health care for people with a learning disability, chaired by Sir Jonathan Michael.

whyNot.0: CIPOLD (2013) was led by the Norah Fry Research Centre.
whyNot.1: Building the Right Support (2015) was a national plan for community services.
whyNot.3: LeDeR is the mortality review programme that followed CIPOLD.

A.q: Ffion is teaching about the Confidential Inquiry into Premature Deaths of People with Learning Disabilities (CIPOLD, 2013). How much earlier did men and women with a learning disability die than the general population?
options: Men about 20 years and women about 13 years
Men about 5 years and women about 8 years
Men and women both about 10 years
Men about 13 years and women about 20 years
A.why: CIPOLD found men with a learning disability died on average 13 years earlier and women 20 years earlier.

whyNot.0: This reverses the figures for men and women.
whyNot.2: CIPOLD found different, larger gaps for men and women.

B.q: Owen, a learning disability liaison nurse, is presenting CIPOLD data to consultants. What proportion of deaths were from causes amenable to good-quality health care?
options: 37% with a learning disability vs 13% in the general population
13% with a learning disability vs 37% in the general population
50% with a learning disability vs 25% in the general population
22% with a learning disability vs 42% in the general population
B.why: CIPOLD found 37% of deaths of people with a learning disability were from causes amenable to good-quality health care, compared with 13% in the general population.

whyNot.3: These are not CIPOLD's figures and reverse the direction of the gap.

B.q: Jodie, new to a community team, learns that a 2011 BBC Panorama programme exposed abuse at Winterbourne View. Which national programme followed in 2012?
options: LeDeR
Valuing People
Healthcare for All
Transforming Care
B.why: Transforming Care (2012) followed Winterbourne View, aiming to move people out of inpatient settings into community support.

whyNot.0: LeDeR followed CIPOLD's recommendation for a mortality review.
whyNot.1: Valuing People was published in 2001, before Winterbourne View.
whyNot.2: Healthcare for All (2008) followed Death by Indifference.

B.q: Nadia is briefing on inpatient care. What was the Building the Right Support action plan target for people with a learning disability and autistic people in inpatient settings?
options: Halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with 2015
Close every assessment and treatment unit by March 2020
Cut inpatient numbers by a quarter by March 2030
Keep each admission under 28 days from March 2022
B.why: The Building the Right Support action plan (2022) aimed to halve inpatient numbers by March 2024 compared with March 2015. The target was missed.

whyNot.1: There was no target to close every unit by 2020.
whyNot.2: This is not the target set in the action plan.
whyNot.3: There was no 28-day limit target in the action plan.

C.q: Marcus, a nurse consultant, explains that one CIPOLD recommendation became a permanent national programme. What was it?
options: A national register of reasonable adjustments
A statutory training requirement for care staff
A national review of the deaths of people with LD
A target to halve the number of inpatients
C.why: CIPOLD recommended a national mortality review body, which became the LeDeR programme.

whyNot.0: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag came much later and from a different route.
whyNot.1: Statutory training followed Oliver McGowan's death and the Health and Care Act 2022.
whyNot.3: The inpatient target came from Building the Right Support.

C.q: Bethan, a ward manager, asks which theme runs through Death by Indifference, CIPOLD and LeDeR so that she can use it in staff training. What is the best answer?
options: Too many people admitted to specialist hospitals
Overuse of community services instead of hospital
Shortages of learning disability nurses in prisons
Delayed diagnosis and treatment, with families not listened to
C.why: All three describe delays in recognising and treating illness and failures to listen to families and carers.

whyNot.0: Inpatient numbers were the focus of Transforming Care, not these mortality reports.
whyNot.1: The reports describe barriers to care, not overuse of community services.
whyNot.2: This was not a theme of these reports.

C.q: A briefing on progress since Building the Right Support asks what had happened to inpatient numbers by February 2025. Which statement is accurate?
options: Numbers fell by about 29% to 2,055; the target was missed
Numbers fell by about 50% to 1,450; the target was met
Numbers rose by about 10% to 3,200 since 2015
Numbers stayed at about 2,900, the 2015 level
C.why: By February 2025 there were 2,055 inpatients, down 29% from 2,905, so the halving target was missed.

whyNot.1: Numbers did not halve; the target was missed.

reteach.title: Two families of reports
reteach.question: How do you keep the reports straight in your head?

blocks.body: One family is about early deaths in health care: Death by Indifference (2007), Healthcare for All (2008), CIPOLD (2013), then LeDeR. The other is about abuse and detention in hospital units: Winterbourne View (2011), Transforming Care (2012), Building the Right Support (2015 and 2022).

blocks.text: CIPOLD: 13 years (men), 20 years (women), 37% vs 13%. Do not reverse them.

explain.body: Mencap, 2007: six people with a learning disability who died in NHS care. It led to Healthcare for All (2008), an independent inquiry chaired by Sir Jonathan Michael.

test.q: How many deaths did Mencap's Death by Indifference describe?
options: Three
Twelve
Six
Twenty
test.why: Death by Indifference told the stories of six people with a learning disability who died in NHS care.

whyNot.0: The report described six deaths, not three.
whyNot.1: The report described six deaths, not twelve.
whyNot.3: The report described six deaths, not twenty.

explain.body: Heslop et al., Norah Fry Research Centre, 2013. Men died 13 years and women 20 years earlier. 37% of deaths were amenable to good care vs 13% in the general population. Recommended a national mortality review: LeDeR.

test.q: Which of these reports measured how much earlier men and women with a learning disability died than the general population in England?
options: CIPOLD
Winterbourne View review
Valuing People
Transforming Care
test.why: CIPOLD (2013) quantified premature deaths: 13 years earlier for men and 20 years for women.

whyNot.1: Winterbourne View concerned abuse in an inpatient unit.
whyNot.3: Transforming Care concerned moving people out of hospital.

explain.body: 2011 BBC Panorama exposed abuse. Transforming Care (2012) and Building the Right Support (2015) aimed to move people into community support. The 2022 action plan target to halve inpatients by March 2024 was missed.

test.q: What exposed the abuse of patients at Winterbourne View in 2011?
options: A CQC routine inspection
A LeDeR mortality review
Undercover filming by BBC Panorama
A Mencap report on six deaths
test.why: A BBC Panorama programme in 2011 used undercover filming to expose the abuse.

whyNot.0: It was exposed by journalists, not a routine inspection.
whyNot.1: LeDeR did not exist then and reviews deaths, not abuse in units.
whyNot.3: Mencap's 2007 report was Death by Indifference.

explain.body: Act on change from baseline, listen to families, look for physical causes before blaming the disability, plan adjustments in advance, and speak up about closed cultures.

test.q: Peter's mother says, 'He is not himself; he usually chats to me.' Which response best reflects the lessons of the landmark reports?
options: Explain that some withdrawal is common in hospital
Ask how he differs from usual and reassess him now
Note her comment and review him at the next round
Suggest she visits less often so he can rest more
test.why: The reports repeatedly found families' concerns were not acted on. A change from baseline reported by family should trigger reassessment now.

whyNot.0: This dismisses a change from baseline as expected.
whyNot.2: Delaying review repeats the delays the reports criticised.
whyNot.3: This discourages the family who know his baseline best.
